newsitem.title: USA: U.S. analysts see rising pressure on Thai baht.
newsitem.headline: U.S. analysts see rising pressure on Thai baht.

text.p: The imminent departure of Thai finance minister Amnuay Viravan is increasing the likelihood of currency devaluation, U.S. analysts and currency traders said.
After months of mounting political pressure, Amnuay is throwing in the towel. His adviser said Amnuay would submit his a letter of resignation on Thursday.
Amnuay's resignation is sending a very negative message to the market, said Feroz Talyarkhan, a managing director at Bear Stearns.
"Because of the political crisis that has developed, the devaluation is more likely now than in the past " he said.
He noted that Amnuay has been the key government figure to hold the finanical and economic picture together since taking office last December. His

In U.S. trading, Amnuay's resignation rumor pushed the spot rate from 22.500 to 23.500 per U.S. dollar, said a trader, who noted that the move still put the baht below the 25.000-mid-point of a band prevailing since the government slapped on exchange control a month ago. AT 1400 EDT/1900 GMT, the baht was quoted 23.700 bid and 23.800 offered.
"The spot has little movement, but the forward is all over the map," said another trader. While the one- two- and three-month forward were bid, one-year was offered, she said.
"People are scared of the volatility," she said, noting that many players had been burned in selling the baht short.
Earlier in Asian trading, the baht rallied to a 16-year high against the dollar at 22.800/000 in the offshore market because of a short squeeze.
Geoffrey Dennis, emerging market analyst at HSBC James Capel, predicted a "cathartic selloff" in the Thai stock market, which could deal a final blow to the two-tier exchange system.

At this point, foreign investors would return only if they believe the Thai market has hit the bottom, he said, noting that the value of the Thai stock market has plunged 75 percent since its peak in 1994.
By devaluating the baht, the Thai government could send a signal to the market that "the worst is over," Dennis said.
Bear Stearns' Talyarkhan doubted that Amnuay's successor could pull out a quick fix.

He said the next finance minister, who is likely to be another unelected official from outside the government, would face the same quandary as Amnuay: High domestic interest rate would continue to crimp the economy without a devaluation, yet a devaluation would inflate the cost of debt servicing to many Thai companies which had issued debt in the overseas market.
Reflecting this somber view, the spread of Thailand's yankee bond over U.S. Treasury widened to 98 basis points (bps), according to trading sources.
The $600 million 10-year bond was priced at 90 bps over Treasury at issuance and traded as tight as 84 bps before losing ground since the financial crisis deepened.
